newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Run on rand seen cutting S.African foreign reserves.
newsitem.headline: Run on rand seen cutting S.African foreign reserves.

text.p: South Africa's rand held steady on Friday after bouncing back from a run of record lows, but economists said central bank intervention in defence of the currency will have depleted already low foreign reserves.

According to a Reuters poll of 11 economists, South Africa's gold and foreign exchange reserves are likely to have shrunk to 9.6 billion rand ($2.05 billion) at the end of October from 10.0 billion a month earlier, or just under four weeks import cover.

Aggressive dollar sales by the Reserve Bank to stabilise the rand will have sliced into official hard currency holdings, more than offsetting an inflow of funds from the proceeds of two international bond issues, they said.
"The Bank probably lost reserves trying to prop up the rand in the latter part of the month," said Peter Perkins, an economist at mining house JCI Ltd.

The exact size of end-October reserves, due to be announced on November 7, will depend on whether the authorities have taken out further loans from foreign banks or paid back money borrowed in September.
Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals said last Monday he had not borrowed any more at that stage, but economists said this could have changed given the turbulence on the foreign exchange markets.
As a result forecasts for October reserves ranged widely, from 9.0 billion rand to 10.5 billion, with most economists predicting a slightly lower number.
The rand ended firmer, but off its strongest levels. At the 1400 GMT close, it was pegged at 4.6835/6985, from 4.7020/7070 after touching the day's strongest level of 4.6550 bid.
Dealers said speculators with long dollar positions were continuing to bale out after the market's whiplash reversal.
The healthier rand also spurred other markets with bond yields falling, though they ended off their lowest levels.
The Johannesburg Stock Exchange overall index lost 3.9 points to close at 6,971.4 points, with golds finishing softer on a weaker bullion price.
The market mood was nervous with anxieties remaining over the balance of payments, low foreign reserves and the government's ambivalence on the lifting of exchange controls.
There were rumours that the authorities might announce moves to ease foreign exchange controls -- possibly backed up by an International Monetary Fund (IMF) package -- at the weekend.

Finance Ministry spokeswoman Jennifer Wilson confirmed that Stals, Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and senior officials were to meet in Cape Town in a routine monthly consultation held on the first Friday of each month. By Friday evening there was no statement from the talks.

There have been mounting calls for the scrapping of rand controls on residents, seen as a major cause of instability in the market because investors try to second-guess a move that could trigger a further capital flight.
However, Stals has said on several occasions in recent days that calls for the immediate scrapping of controls were unreasonable while reserves remain precariously low.
